2026-09-07.headline: Score HOLDS at 27/30 for a twentieth consecutive edition. No channel moved. One. The war became navy-on-navy, and for the FIRST time in this war CENTCOM published a target list with a battle damage assessment. Iran fired ballistic missiles at TWO US Navy warships — a carrier and a guided-missile destroyer — on 5 September; CENTCOM says both evaded and no American was harmed. It then destroyed THREE Iranian tankers and NAMED them with damage assessments: Downy off Kharg and Stark 1 near Jask permanently disabled, Kylo ‘completely destroyed’, which JMIC 094 logs as sunk. ‘Tanker for tanker’, carried here for two editions as ONE anonymous sourcing chain at TIER 2, is now the theatre commander’s own stated policy on the record — the caveat is DISCHARGED in the direction of confirmation. Iran’s answer is not: its claim to have struck three tankers is UNCORROBORATED — JMIC 094 records NIL new incidents, the count is frozen at 101, no vessel is named, no UKMTO product corroborates it, and CENTCOM called the separate drone-boat claim a lie. (!) 094’s cut-off is 051500Z, so it is SILENT on 6 September. Two. The oil trigger took a THIRD close. The ACTIVE contract closed $96.28 on 4 September after $95.63 and $95.52 — its highest close since 26 May — while the SCORED continuation closed $92.32, $2.68 below $95 and NARROWED from $3.37, the nearest since 21 August. Three consecutive closes is past any reading of sustained. The rule is written on the continuation and is NOT moved to the series that would fire it (§9.26, §9.56b). Oil holds at 2/5 and the other reading is published, not suppressed. Three. Iran began writing the geometry alone. Its security-council secretary said on 6 September that Iran will declare an exclusion zone running from the American blockade line into the Gulf, with entrants added to its own sanctions list, and that Hormuz maps are agreed with Oman and will be signed. OMAN HAS PUBLISHED NOTHING CONFIRMING IT. fm.gov.om read direct: nothing dated 5–7 September, and the last item on its statements page is the 25 August joint statement; and Oman’s foreign minister wrote on 4 September that no solution has been reached. A bilateral instrument carrying one signatory’s text is the 26 August failure repeating. Four, and it is the pump. US retail diesel TOOK ITS ALL-TIME RECORD — AAA $5.85 on 4 September, through the $5.8159 of 19 June 2022, and reset again on 5 and 6 September, to $5.8819 and $5.8970. The last edition put it 3.27 cents away. It is the FIRST US retail fuel price to exceed a pre-war all-time high in this war, and the political channel cannot see it. August payrolls printed +162,000 against a ~53,000 consensus with +55,000 of upward revisions; the curve answered with a BEAR FLATTENER and September hike odds went 48.4% to 58.4% on one venue’s series. MOVE 73.10, a SECOND sub-75 close and below its own pre-war anchor. Sequencing 27 → 27 → 27 → 27 → 27.

bondYield.title: MARITIME DENIAL — 5/5, held. The incident count froze while the water emptied, and the mine deletion survived a second issue.
bondYield.text: (i) The state. The downgrade requires a verified reopening AND traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. Neither leg advanced: no reopening occurred, and the traffic leg moved the wrong way. JMIC Update 094 was issued on 6 September (ICOD 051500Z), Hormuz stays SEVERE, every regional threat level is unchanged from 093, and the five held merchant vessels are the same five. (ii) The confirmed-incident count is FROZEN at 101 — NIL since 093 — and that frozen number is the load-bearing fact of this section. Iran claimed on 5 September to have struck three tankers on an ‘unauthorised’ route plus several US-linked vessels, and separately on 6 September to have hit a US uncrewed vessel. No vessel is named, no flag, no damage report; JMIC records no incident; and UKMTO issued no warning or advisory on 6 or 7 September on a direct read of both 2026 listings. (!) BOUND IT: 094’s ICOD is 051500Z, so the frozen count contradicts the 5 September claim only for the window it covers and is SILENT on 6 September. (!) The three tankers the UNITED STATES struck are in the record, as ADVISORY 127-26 A/B/C, and JMIC classes them expressly as a military-on-listed-tanker event rather than an attack on a third-flag merchant, so they do NOT enter the 101 — a distinction this document adopts rather than blurs. (iii) THE MINE DELETION IS NO LONGER AN EDITING ARTEFACT. The last edition’s watchlist asked whether 094 would restore the danger-area language 091 and 092 carried. It did not: 094 reproduces 093’s weaker ‘remain vigilant for mining activity’ formula VERBATIM, with no declared area, no coordinates and no NAVCENT clearance sentence. Two consecutive issues make it more than an editing artefact. (!) It is NOT yet settled — on this document’s own §9.18 standard, applied symmetrically, two observations are a run and not a regime, and 095 decides whether it holds a third issue. It is still not a declaration that the mines are gone: the allied record has gone quiet on mines, which is weaker evidence in BOTH directions. (iv) The traffic leg is measurable and it deteriorated on the series that published. (!) Bound it: PortWatch is UNCHANGED at 7% of typical and a week stale, Windward is NOT FOUND for this window, and the facilitated series ROSE. Kpler puts the ten-day moving average at 10 transits a day on 6 September, the lowest since May, with two on Saturday and six on Sunday, mostly on the Iranian route; one VLCC entered on Sunday and none has exited since Wednesday 2 September; LSEG has a Saudi products tanker turning back on 6 September. JMIC’s own annex gives 0, 5 and 1 across 3–5 September on non-facilitated cargo vessels, against 59 US NCAGS-facilitated transits over a window JMIC labels 3–5 September and calls 48 hours, against 44 and 39 on the two prior reports. (!) The label and the dates disagree, so no per-day rate is computed and no ranking is asserted. 094 is the first issue to NAME the split in its own text, contrasting single-digit independent tracking with NCAGS traffic averaging over twenty a day. Naming a discrepancy is not reconciling it, and this document still publishes both with their universes attached (§9.24). (v) The blockade tally moved a second consecutive edition, to 87 redirected / 3 disabled / 2 boarded, CENTCOM-dated 3 September. A circulating ‘about 90’ is a press paraphrase that could not be sourced to any CENTCOM release and is NOT used (§9.19).

bondYield.title: OIL PRICE SHOCK — 2/5, held. A THIRD consecutive close above the level on the active contract, and the scored series moved TOWARD it. The rule still names one price and there are still two.
bondYield.text: (i) §9.56 is now three closes old and the arithmetic has stopped being arguable. The active contract closed $95.63, $95.52 and $96.28 on 2, 3 and 4 September — three consecutive confirmed closes above $95, and the highest active close since 26 May. Two closes is this instrument’s own definition of a sustained break; three is past it. Applied to COA the oil upgrade fired last week. Applied to CO2, the series the rule has always been read on, it has not: the continuation closed $92.32, +$0.69, $2.68 below the level. (ii) The rule is NOT moved, and this edition removes the one comfort the last one had. On 3 September the scored series moved AWAY while the active stayed through, which made it easy to say the trigger had not nearly fired. This session both moved the same way: the scored gap NARROWED from $3.37 to $2.68, the nearest reading since the 21 August close left $2.33 — that close was never an edition’s scoring reference, so its $2.33 is not among the fourteen — while the active extended. There is no longer a divergence to hide behind — only a rule written on the wider of two series that are both rising. It is not moved because moving it would be moving it to the series that fires it (§9.26, §9.56b). (iii) Bound the claim and correct the count. This is the active contract’s first RUN OF THREE closes above $95 since 20–22 May. (!) It has now closed above the level TWENTY-SIX times in this war; the last edition published twenty-six as the count through 3 September, which was one too high, and that figure is CORRECTED to twenty-five (§9.32). (iv) The basis is stable and the roll was clean. Brent’s has run 0.00, 2.12, 3.08, 3.54, 3.89, 3.96 — one step off zero at the 31 August roll, then FOUR sessions of decelerating widening, +0.96, +0.46, +0.35, +0.07, with no second step and no sign change. (!) WTI’s independent basis NARROWED on the same session, 3.27 to 2.91, which is an argument against reading either basis as a market signal rather than a roll artefact. §9.41 clears; §9.36 still forbids constructing anything across the two Brent series. (v) The price is not being set in the Gulf alone. OPEC+ held October output UNCHANGED on 6 September at a 31.1 mb/d target, ending six consecutive monthly increases, and no September IEA or OPEC monthly report had been published at the cut — both are PROSPECTIVE, not NOT OBTAINED (§9.46).

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. The firing trigger held a fourth close but on its narrowest margin of the run, and the labour print reversed the front end.
bondYield.text: (i) The 5y5y forward closed 2.3082%, −0.72 bp, a FOURTH consecutive close above the 2.30% firing level — but by the NARROWEST margin of the four. The run reads 1.10, 0.96, 1.54, 0.82 bp. A margin of 0.82 bp is inside a single session’s typical move and is reported as such rather than as clearance. The scored downgrade, the 2.142% anchor, is 16.62 bp away and has not been approached in this window. §9.26 has paid twice already and the rule is not rewritten to the firing level now that the margin is thin. (ii) The composition inverted again, and it is REAL yield for a second session. The 10-year nominal ROSE 1.41 bp while BE10 FELL 0.07 to 2.3532% — so the whole rise and more came out of real yield, the mirror of 3 September when the whole fall did. BE10 sits 9.63 bp above its 2.2569% anchor. The two breakeven measures moved the same way as each other for a second consecutive session (§9.54). (iii) The hard print of the window is the labour market and it landed AFTER the last cut, exactly as flagged. August payrolls +162,000 against a consensus near 53,000, unemployment unchanged at 4.1%, average hourly earnings +0.3% m/m and +3.1% y/y — with June and July revised UP a combined +55,000 and July flipping from −23,000 to +21,000. (!) The reaction function is INVERTED and behaved as this document said it would: a strong print is the hawkish outcome. CME-implied odds of a 25 bp HIKE on 16 September ran 66.1% on 31 August, 48.4% on 3 September after a governor’s remarks and 58.4% on 4 September after payrolls — ONE outlet’s series, held throughout. (!) A second outlet read 49.4% on 3 September and is NOT spliced into it (§9.24). (iv) The services survey of 3 September stands behind it: ISM Services 55.4 with Prices Paid 72.6, the fifth reading above 70 in six months, against Employment contracting a second month at 47.8. (!) The two point DIFFERENT WAYS and are not merged: the services employment index is already contracting while the aggregate payrolls print ran hot. What is not in dispute is the input-cost shock arriving in the largest part of the US economy.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. The volatility leg is satisfied a SECOND close and is now below its pre-war anchor; the yield leg is 24 bp away and Threshold B armed a sixth time on diverging legs.
bondYield.text: (i) MOVE closed 73.10, −1.58 — a SECOND consecutive close below 75, and the first close BELOW the 73.38 pre-war anchor since 28 August. The last edition’s watchlist asked whether one sub-75 close would become two; it did. The downgrade needs the 30-year below 5.00% WITH MOVE below 75, sustained; the yield leg fails by 24.23 bp, narrowed from 24.65. (ii) (!) §9.18 is not discharged by two closes, and the yield leg has not been within 15 bp of its condition since 28 July nor closed below 5.00% since 6 July. The longest sub-75 run SINCE THE CURRENT REGIME BEGAN on 29 July is NINE closes, 18–28 August, and it ended in a single session on 31 August with MOVE at 75.32; the leg was satisfied and given back inside one session on 5 and on 7 August. (!) Bounded properly (§9.32): the war’s longest sub-75 run is TWENTY-ONE closes, 10 June–10 July, in a regime that no longer obtains. Two closes is the start of a run, not a regime, and the yield leg has never come within 15 bp of its condition. (iii) (!) THE ANOMALY IS BACK. Treasury volatility is now 0.28 points BELOW its pre-war anchor while the 30-year sits 63.17 bp ABOVE its own. That is a fully normalised expectation of movement around a yield that has not normalised at all — the configuration this document described in August, closed on 31 August, and now records again. The two deviations are reported separately and no composite is constructed. (iv) The curve shape was a BEAR FLATTENER falling monotonically with tenor — 2Y +3.01 bp, 5Y +3.04, 10Y +1.41, 30Y −0.42 — with 2s10s −1.394 corroborating independently. This is a Fed repricing, not a Hormuz one, and it is the FIRST bear flattener since 1 September, the third distinct curve signature in the five sessions since 31 August. Every war-high close set on 1 September at the 2-, 5- and 10-year SURVIVES, and the 5-year came within 1.03 bp of taking its own. (!) The 30-year fell BECAUSE the front end rose: a market pricing a hike into a supply shock is pricing a central bank defending its target, which lifts the near path and leaves the far one. (v) The week ahead is the test. A $58bn 3-year on 8 September, a $39bn 10-year reopening on 9 September and a $22bn 30-year reopening on 10 September — $119bn of coupons, all settling 15 September, the first day of the FOMC — and the enlarged long-end buyback regime begins on 9 September, the same day as the 10-year. August CPI on 11 September was named by a Federal Reserve governor as the swing input for the 15–16 September decision. (!) No trend is read from $22bn against August’s $25bn: a reopening is not a new issue (§9.40).

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series backfilled up to a three-month high, and the fuel that was three cents from an all-time record took it.
bondYield.text: (i) The scored series moved AWAY from its downgrade for a fourth consecutive edition. AUTMUSAG BACKFILLED UP to $4.92  for 3 September against the $4.90 carried as last resolved — a FIFTH consecutive rise and the highest print since 29 May, expressly NOT a war high ($5.18, 20 May). It sits 32 cents above the $4.60 downgrade condition and 17 above the $4.75 that fired the upgrade. The 4 and 7 September cells are dark and are not extrapolated (§9.30). (ii) THE RECORD FELL, AND THE INSTRUMENT COULD NOT REGISTER IT. The last edition put AAA diesel 3.27 cents below its all-time record of $5.8159 of 19 June 2022. It printed $5.85 the next day, 4 September, taking the record; then $5.8819 and $5.8970. AAA’s own highest-recorded-price table, read direct on 7 September, now carries $5.8970 set 6 September 2026 and no longer displays the 2022 figure. This is the first US retail fuel price to exceed a pre-war all-time high in this war. Gasoline did not follow — AAA regular $4.1473 against its own $5.0165 record of 14 June 2022 — and the divergence widened: +29.35c on the week for diesel against +6.86c for regular, more than four times the pace for a second consecutive edition. (iii) The cause is a US refining constraint, not a crude one, and it is legible in the EIA weekly for the week ending 28 August: distillate stocks 104.2 mn bbl, 14% below the five-year average and 10.1% below the same week of 2025, against refinery utilisation of 98%, the highest since August 2018. A system running at 98% has nothing left with which to rebuild a distillate stock that a chokepoint keeps draining. (!) There is a second, non-Hormuz driver and it must be named rather than absorbed: a Russian diesel export suspension following strikes on Russian refineries. The document does not apportion between the two. (iv) The limitation is the finding, and it is sharper than a slow-moving series. The political channel is scored on AUTMUSAG, which produced NO PRINT AT ALL in the record window — dark on 4 and 7 September, its last resolved value a two-cent backfill dated 3 September, before the record was set. The record was set in a fuel the trigger cannot see, and the $3.52 anchor and the whole scored history are written on the series that moved least. That is stated rather than corrected, because re-basing a trigger to the series that would move it is what §9.21 and §9.56b forbid.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. Iran fired ballistic missiles at two US warships, the US sank a tanker in reply, and the mediator was again the missing signature.
bondYield.text: (i) THE EXCHANGE BECAME DIRECT AND NAVAL, AND THE UNITED STATES PUBLISHED IT. CENTCOM’s 5 September release — its first since 1 September and only its second since 15 August — states that the IRGC launched ballistic missiles toward a carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, that both evaded and that no American was harmed. It then names three Iranian tankers destroyed in reply, each with a damage assessment: Downy off Kharg and Stark 1 near Jask permanently disabled, Kylo sunk in the Gulf of Oman, with strike video released. (!) This is the first CENTCOM product of the war carrying a target list AND a BDA, and this document has spent three editions asking for exactly that. (ii) A STANDING CAVEAT IS DISCHARGED, AND IN THE DIRECTION OF CONFIRMATION. ‘Tanker for tanker’ was carried on 3 and 4 September as TIER 2 — anonymous officials, one outlet, no named confirmation or denial. It is now the theatre commander’s own stated policy, on the record and on CENTCOM’s own site. The Secretary of Defense said the same in public the same day. TIER 2 becomes TIER 1. (iii) Iran’s half of the exchange is the opposite. methodology.intraday: §9.56 — NOW THREE CLOSES OLD, AND THE LAST DEFENCE OF THE STATUS QUO HAS GONE. A trigger written on a continuation series stops being well-defined the moment the basis opens, and the failure is silent. The oil channel’s upgrade is ‘Brent above $95 sustained’. That rule was written and applied through long stretches in which CO2 and COA printed the SAME NUMBER — most recently exactly zero for twenty consecutive sessions to 28 August. Earlier rolls opened a basis too; what is new is a roll that opened one STRADDLING the trigger. Brent rolled on 31 August and the basis has widened on every session since: 2.12, 3.08, 3.54, 3.89, 3.96. On the 4 September close the trigger falls BETWEEN the two series for a THIRD consecutive session: the scored continuation is $2.68 below it and the active contract $1.28 ABOVE it. ‘Sustained’ has a settled operational meaning here — two consecutive confirmed closes, the test that fired US-inflation 4→5 on 31 July and cut oil 2→1 on 3 July. The active contract has now closed above $95 THREE times in succession, so on that series the upgrade condition is met in full and has been since the 3 September close. (!) THE MATERIAL CHANGE THIS EDITION IS THAT THE TWO SERIES NOW POINT THE SAME WAY. On 3 September the scored series moved AWAY while the active stayed through, and that divergence was a real reason to hold calmly. On 4 September both rose and the scored gap NARROWED to its nearest reading since 21 August. The hold now rests on nothing except which series the rule happens to be written on, and that is stated plainly rather than dressed up. Three things follow and all three remain the practice. (a) The channel is held on the scored continuation, and the alternative reading is published in the EDITION rather than buried here, because a reader checking a screen quote for ‘Brent’ will find the active contract. (b) The rule is NOT moved to whichever series would fire it — the §9.26 discipline. (c) The problem is disclosed as an open methodological question and NOT decided under the pressure of a fired trigger, which is the §9.16 precedent. The general form, which will recur: any threshold expressed as an absolute level on a rolling series has an undefined region as wide as the basis, and the basis is zero exactly when nobody is looking at it. ¶ §9.51 — CARRIED FORWARD, UNCHANGED AND UNSETTLED, and now six observations deep. When a defective test is met a second time by a different mechanism, record the MECHANISM, not a verdict. §9.49 recorded Threshold B’s 28 August arming as a defect: a long-end stress test tripped by an 11.14 bp front-end move in which the 30-year contributed 1.25 bp. On 31 August B held on a bear STEEPENER in which the 30-year contributed the largest move on the curve; on 1 September on a bear FLATTENER in which it contributed the smallest; on 2 and 3 September on a BULL STEEPENER twice; and on 4 September on a bear flattener again, in which the 30-year was the ONLY tenor to FALL. (!) The written test has now returned the same answer through three of the four configurations available, in both directions, and on the latest occasion it was satisfied while its own long-end leg moved TOWARD the threshold, the margin narrowing 4.65 to 4.23 bp — the test held open by the leg it was not written about. That is not ambiguity observed twice but six times, and it strengthens rather than resolves the original complaint. (!) A second observation sharpens it further, and it is new this edition: the two legs DIVERGED for the first time in the run — the 30-year margin narrowed a third consecutive close to 4.23 bp while the 10-year’s WIDENED to 13.21 bp — so a single test is now being held open by the leg it was not written about. The open question is unchanged and is not settled here: whether B should be conditioned on a long-end CONTRIBUTION rather than a long-end LEVEL. ¶ Restatements and comparability. Vendor restatements are normal and make absolute levels non-comparable across editions, though directional analysis is continuous. A contract roll does the same thing to a continuation series silently, which is why the basis check is a standing check. The dual gasoline series is never re-based: AUTMUSAG is the scored reference and preserves the $3.52 anchor and the $4.75 trigger; USRFRUSA is corroboration only; AAA’s published headline is a third series and is never compared with either. The pre-war anchor is the 27 February 2026 close, re-verified field by field every edition; it is unchanged to date. FOUR OPEN ITEMS REMAIN DISCLOSED RATHER THAN DECIDED. (1) FIRST IN LINE AND SHARPER THAN LAST EDITION: §9.56, the oil trigger’s ambiguity across the roll — $2.68 below on the scored series and $1.28 through on the active one, with three consecutive closes through on the active series and, for the first time, both series moving the same way. (2) Threshold B’s long-end LEVEL versus long-end CONTRIBUTION question, per §9.49 and §9.51, now six observations deep with diverging legs and a narrowing 30-year margin. (3) §9.57, the reconciliation of the scored gasoline series to any published construction, open and un-advanceable this edition. (4) The US-inflation channel’s firing-versus-downgrade gap, no longer dormant: the firing trigger has held four closes but the margin has narrowed to 0.82 bp while the downgrade sits 16.62 bp lower. The oil channel’s own separate asymmetry stands unchanged: its downgrade is written as a mediated pause AND ‘a close’ at or below $72.48 while its upgrade requires a SUSTAINED break, which as written makes the downgrade’s PRICE limb easier to trip than the upgrade’s, though the downgrade also requires a mediated pause and is not therefore the easier test overall. It is $19.84 away and not live.

(!) ‘NORMAL’ HAS NO SINGLE DENOMINATOR — Kpler’s pre-war ~130–140/day, IMF PortWatch’s 85/day — and on NEITHER does current traffic clear 25%; the nearest reading of the war is UKMTO VRA’s 22–23% to 27 August, itself twelve days stale. The leg is not close. Neither leg advanced and the traffic leg moved sharply the wrong way. (ii) The adjudicating document is MISSING, and that is the honest description. No JMIC Update 095 exists at the cut on a direct read of ukmto.org, so 094’s frozen count of 101, cut off at 051500Z, is SILENT on 6, 7 and 8 September and cannot be used to test anything that happened in them. It is PROSPECTIVE, not NOT OBTAINED (§9.46). The only UKMTO product since is ADVISORY 127-26 of 6 September, which JMIC maps onto the three tankers the UNITED STATES struck — so the newest item in the maritime record is the American action, not an Iranian one. (!) Iran’s 5 September claim to have struck three tankers is therefore UNCORROBORATED into a fourth day, and the correct statement is that no allied product records it, not that no such attack occurred. (iii) The traffic leg deteriorated on the one series that publishes daily, and the readings cannot be joined. Kpler published three ten-day moving averages of visible commodity vessels — above 15 on 4 September, about 13 on the 5th, 10 on the 6th — and calls the last its lowest since May, publishing no numeric May baseline, so the superlative is the PROVIDER’S and is not independently checkable. (!) A ten-day mean cannot move five points in two sessions, so these are not one series: each is reported as a separate provider reading and NO rate of change and no direction is computed across them (§9.24). There is no 7 or 8 September reading from any provider. (iv) A CLAIM THIS DOCUMENT CARRIED IS WITHDRAWN. Last edition said no VLCC had exited since 2 September. Kpler still says that of its VISIBLE universe; Windward’s AIS-plus-dark log records a 340-metre VLCC-class tanker outbound on 4 September, dark, at reduced speed, trailing a 16km sheen. A dark hull cannot appear in a visible count, so the two are reconcilable and the unqualified form was wrong. The claim is re-issued as no VISIBLE VLCC exit since 2 September (§9.19, §9.24). (v) THREE CENTCOM-dated readings in four days, two moves: 87 on 3 September, 92 on 6 September, 94 on 7 September, with disabled and boarded unchanged at 3 and 2 throughout. (!) The point is not the seven vessels. It is that JMIC 094 cited 87 as the latest available official figure on the day it published, when CENTCOM’s own count was already 92 — the allied summary is a lagging record of the American operation, and this document will not treat it as a check on it.

bondYield.text: (i) §9.56 has run out of mitigating detail. The active contract has now closed above $95 on FOUR consecutive sessions — $95.63, $95.52, $96.28, $97.00 — the last being the highest active close since 22 May, and the first run of four since a twenty-close run ended on that date. Two closes is this instrument’s own definition of a sustained break. Applied to COA, the upgrade condition was met on the 3 September close — five days ago. (ii) Applied to CO2, the series the rule has always been read on, it has not: the continuation closed $93.16, +$0.84, $1.84 below the level. But that is now the nearest this series has closed to $95 since it was last ABOVE it on 24 July, and it narrowed from $2.68. On 3 September the two series moved apart, which made the hold comfortable; on 7 September they moved together, and the gap has narrowed 45% across two sessions — $3.37, $2.68, $1.84. (iii) The rule is NOT moved, and there is an AFFIRMATIVE reason as well as a procedural one. The affirmative reason: the $95 upgrade, the $72.48 downgrade and the $72.48 pre-war anchor are ALL written on the continuation, so moving the upgrade alone to COA would leave the downgrade and the anchor on a different series and make the channel incoherent in the other direction. The procedural reason: moving it now would be moving it to the series that fires it, six days and four closes after the document disclosed the problem in the open. That is exactly what §9.26 forbids and what §9.16 anticipated. The score is held, the alternative reading is printed in the tape, in the score grid and in the watchlist, and a reader who checks a screen quote for ‘Brent’ will find $97.00 and can see why. (!) What would settle it is not an argument but a print: two CO2 closes above $95 fires the upgrade on the rule as written, and $1.84 is roughly two sessions’ worth of the recent move — the largest daily change on this series in the last four sessions is $0.84. (iv) The basis is stable and neither leg is a signal. Brent’s ran 3.89, 3.96, 3.84, 3.88 across 3–8 September — a narrowing then a part-retrace, with no second step and no sign change; WTI’s went 2.91 on 4 September to 3.07 on the 8 September mark, a widening, with no 7 September value at all. (!) Two contracts moving opposite ways across the same span for a second consecutive edition is an argument against reading either basis as a market signal. §9.41 clears; §9.36 still forbids constructing anything across the two Brent series. (v) The move is not being made in the Gulf alone. OPEC+ held October output UNCHANGED on 6 September, and its stated reason was that it must first review member capacity to set 2027 baselines — a process, not a barrel. (!) No quantified OPEC+ spare-capacity figure dated 4–8 September was published or found, and none is scheduled — an absence in the record rather than a pending release or a retrieval failure. The September STEO is due 9 September and the WPSR 10 September, both delayed by the holiday.

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. The count of closes above the firing level did not advance, because there was no close; and the breakeven has now failed to resolve on two consecutive rows.
bondYield.text: (i) The 5y5y forward count STAYS AT FOUR. Its last resolved value is the 4 September close of 2.3082%, 0.82 bp above the 2.30% firing level and the narrowest of the four. There was no 7 September close, so no fifth close exists and none is claimed. The 8 September mark of 2.3030% would leave 0.30 bp — but a mark decides nothing, and this document has been wrong before by treating one as though it did (§9.31). The scored downgrade, the 2.142% anchor, is 16.62 bp away and has not been approached. (ii) BE10 IS UNRESOLVED ON TWO CONSECUTIVE ROWS, FOR TWO DIFFERENT REASONS, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. On 7 September it was carried because the cash market was shut (§9.58c). On 8 September it printed 2.3536, identical to four decimal places to the 7 September cell, in a row where every nominal tenor moved — which is the pure §9.35 case, the one that concealed a war high on 17 August. Its last RESOLVED value is the 4 September 2.3532%, 9.63 bp above the 2.2569 anchor. (!) §9.48 applies and is stated rather than assumed: an exact repeat on a four-decimal derived generic is strong evidence of a carry, so the rule discriminates well here, and no d/d is asserted either way. (iii) AN INDEPENDENT SERIES SAYS THE SAME THING, AND THE HONEST FORM IS BOUNDED BY A DATE. A Treasury par-curve read puts the 10-year breakeven flat at 2.35% on 1, 2, 3 and 4 September — two decimals, so it cannot separate 2.3532 from 2.3536, and it is quoted for DIRECTION only. Through 4 September, the last date on which either the extract’s breakeven or the par curve resolves, ten-year inflation compensation was flat to two decimals against an ISM services prices-paid index at 72.6, its highest in four years. (!) The diesel records of 4, 6 and 7 September and the $97.00 close of the 7th fall AFTER that date and are UNTESTED by any breakeven reading this document holds. No inference about re-anchoring is available, and none is drawn. (iv) That is corroborated from the podium. A Federal Reserve governor said on 3 September, the last speech before the blackout opened on 5 September: his earlier worry that higher energy prices would bleed into many goods and services prices ‘hasn’t come to pass, at least so far’. He also said it may not take much acceleration to nudge him toward supporting tighter policy, and that his vote turns on August inflation. Those two sentences are the whole September debate, and they are hike-versus-hold, not hold-versus-cut. (v) The pricing supports a BAND and not a direction. Sourceable readings of the September HIKE probability, each with its own outlet and never joined: about 50% (28 Aug), 66% and 70% from two outlets (31 Aug), about 52% (4 Sep, post-payrolls), 59% (5 Sep); a prediction market read 50% on the 5th. (!) THE PRECISE PAIR THE LAST EDITION PUBLISHED — 48.4% then 58.4% — COULD NOT BE RE-VERIFIED AND THE DECIMALS ARE WITHDRAWN (§9.13). (!) NOR does a direction survive: on these numbers the 4 September post-payrolls reading is BELOW both 31 August readings, and deriving a trend from single points on three venues is the splice §9.24 forbids. September hike pricing sits somewhere in a 50–70% band and cannot be narrowed.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. The volatility leg is UNRESOLVED, not satisfied a third time: MOVE has not printed for two sessions, and a stale low is not reassurance.
bondYield.text: (i) MOVE has NO PRINT for 7 or 8 September. Its last close is 73.10 on 4 September, a second consecutive close below 75 and the first below the 73.38 pre-war anchor since 28 August. The downgrade’s volatility leg is therefore satisfied on the last resolved close and UNRESOLVED thereafter — it is NOT satisfied a third session, and this document will not convert a missing print into a close. §9.9 was written for exactly this: MOVE went dark through a 10.9 bp long-end move in July and the stale low read as calm. (ii) The yield leg fails by 24.23 bp on the same close. It has not closed below 5.00% since 6 July. (!) BOUND THE OTHER HALF PROPERLY, because the last edition did not: the claim that the leg ‘has not been within 15 bp since 28 July’ is true of this regime and is NOT a war-long claim — the pre-war anchor of 4.6106% sits 39 bp INSIDE the condition, so the leg was satisfied for the whole of the period before the war. The bounded form is the only honest one. (iii) (!) THE ANOMALY IS UNRESOLVED RATHER THAN PRESENT, and the distinction matters. On the last resolved closes, volatility sits 0.28 points BELOW its anchor while the 30-year sits 63.17 bp ABOVE its own. Both legs of that comparison are now stale by two sessions on one side and unresolved on the other, so it is restated as of 4 September and no live reading is claimed. (iv) The curve, on marks and across TWO sessions rather than one: 2Y +0.66 bp, 5Y +0.54, 10Y +0.41, 20Y +0.13, 30Y +0.21, with 2s10s −0.250. A mild bear flattener in shape — front-led, with the 2s10s at −0.250 consistent BY CONSTRUCTION rather than independently, since 41.144 is 4.7862 minus 4.3727. (!) It is NOT monotonic with tenor: the 30-year rose more than the 20-year. (!) And it is small: the largest move on the curve is two-thirds of a basis point across two trading sessions spanning four calendar days, which after August payrolls of +162,000 with +55,000 of upward revisions — about five times the twelve-month trailing average of +31,000, and 2.5 to 3.1 times a consensus RANGE of 53,000 to 65,000 — is itself the observation. Every war-high close set on 1 September survives; on the last resolved close the 5-year sits 1.03 bp from its own and on the 8 September mark 0.49 bp, the nearest of any tenor on either basis. (v) The supply test is running as this edition is written. A $58bn 3-year auctions on 8 September, a $39bn 10-year reopening on 9 September and a $22bn 30-year reopening on 10 September — $119bn of coupons, all settling 15 September, the first day of the FOMC. (!) Results for none of them exist at the cut. August CPI lands 11 September, inside the blackout.

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series was DARK across the whole record window, and the record it could not see was set three times in four days.
bondYield.text: (i) The scored series moved AWAY from its downgrade for a fifth consecutive edition, then stopped reporting. (!) The downgrade is not a single level: it needs THREE consecutive closes at or below $4.60 with no intervening print above $4.70, so with the series dark the earliest possible move is at least three prints away. AUTMUSAG BACKFILLED to $4.93 for 4 September — a FIFTH consecutive rise and the highest print since 29 May — (!) and the last edition’s ordinal for $4.92 was one too high and is CORRECTED from a fifth to a FOURTH (§9.32), expressly NOT a war high ($5.18, 20 May). It sits 33 cents above the $4.60 downgrade condition and 18 above the $4.75 that fired the upgrade. It produced NO PRINT on 7 or 8 September and is not extrapolated (§9.30). (ii) THE RECORD KEPT FALLING WHILE THE MEASURE WAS DARK. AAA’s national diesel average set a fresh all-time high on 4, 6 and 7 September — $5.8500, $5.8970, $5.9015 — and AAA’s own highest-recorded-price table now shows the current print as the record. (!) Two housekeeping corrections follow from re-verification rather than from news. The superseded 2022 figure is no longer displayed by AAA, so this document stops asserting 19 June 2022 as its date and carries only the level. And the $5.8819 the last edition published for 5 September could not be independently re-verified and is carried as single-source (§9.13). (iii) Gasoline still does not follow. AAA regular $4.1505 on 7 September is 17.3% below its own $5.0165 record of 14 June 2022. On AAA’s own 31 August base, diesel is +30.13c on the week and regular +6.98c — 4.3 times the pace, a third consecutive edition. (!) A FOURTH retail series must not be spliced in: EIA’s on-highway diesel read $5.599 for 31 August against an EIA all-time high of $5.810, so on the EIA series the record has NOT been taken. Different survey, different universe, and its next print is 9 September (§9.19). (iv) The cause is still a refining constraint rather than a crude one, on the 28 August week: distillate stocks 104.2 mn bbl, 14% below the five-year average, against refinery utilisation of 98%, the highest since 2018; and East Coast distillate at 19.318 mn bbl, the lowest in a weekly series that begins in 1990. A Russian diesel export ban, extended on 29 August to 30 September, is a second driver and this document does not apportion between them. (v) THE LIMITATION IS A SCOPE CHOICE, NOT AN INSTRUMENT FAILURE, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS. The scored series resolved on 4 September, the FIRST of the three record days, and was dark on the 7th and 8th — so it saw one of the three and missed two. The deeper point is that AUTMUSAG is a GASOLINE series and the records were in DIESEL, and this document insists in four places that gasoline and diesel are different grades, different surveys and different universes that must never be compared. The channel cannot register a diesel record BY CONSTRUCTION, and its own §1.3 shows why: gasoline did not follow, at 17.3% below its own 2022 record. (!) Whether the political channel should be scored on a distillate series is a real question and is NOT decided here, because re-basing a trigger onto the series that would move it is what §9.21 and §9.56b forbid.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. Iran escalated in words from three institutions in three days and in deeds not at all; Oman is again the missing signature, for a second edition.
bondYield.text: (i) THE KINETIC RECORD SINCE 5 SEPTEMBER IS EMPTY AND THE RHETORICAL ONE IS NOT. No CENTCOM release since 5 September on a direct read of its index; no acknowledged US strike on Iranian SOIL since 1 September, a seventh day; and no Iranian attack on any Gulf state since 3 September. (!) Bound both. The window is NOT kinetically quiet — US forces destroyed three Iranian tankers on 5 September, Iran claims three more, UKMTO logged disabling fire on the 6th and Jizan was struck on the 7th. And the tanker Downy was struck at the Kharg anchorage on 5 September, inside Iranian territorial waters, so the soil claim is a soil-versus-waters distinction rather than an absolute; no damage ashore was reported. (ii) Against that emptiness, three Iranian principals in three days: the parliament speaker on 6 September that the era of proportionate responses is over and that American oil and gas companies across these waters ‘share that exposure’; the security-council secretary on 7 September that the posture toward US warships and bases has been ‘fundamentally recalibrated’; the acting defence minister on 8 September, answering US claims that Iran cannot reach the blockading warships, ‘you will see the results’. All three are announcements. §9.11 governs: an announcement is not an event, and the channel is not moved on any of them — in either direction. (iii) Iran’s 5 September claim to have struck three tankers stays UNCORROBORATED into a fourth day; the newest UKMTO product is the one that logs the AMERICAN strikes. (!) The reported 4 September attack on US targets in JORDAN is STILL UNCONFIRMED on a second day, addressed by no government, and is never merged with the confirmed 31 August and 1 September Jordan events (§9.13). (iv) THE MEDIATOR IS THE MISSING SIGNATURE FOR A SECOND CONSECUTIVE EDITION, AND THE NEGATIVE IS NOW STRONGER, NOT WEAKER. Iran’s security-council secretary said on 6 September that Hormuz maps are agreed with Oman and will be signed within days; its foreign-ministry spokesman said on 7 September that the deal is in its final stages. (!) The method, stated in full: fm.gov.om homepage, Statements archive and on-site search for ‘Hormuz’, all read direct on 8 September. The site is CURRENT and not stale — its own footer reads last updated 7 September 2026 — and the three items it carries for that date are a Rwandan state visit and the Arab League. That distinction is the whole point of §9.23: a silence from a live publisher is evidence; a silence from a dead page is not. Neither confirmation nor denial exists. (v) And the counterparty that matters most has spoken against it: Washington has said it would not recognise an Iran–Oman agreement on the strait, and the State Department said on 8 September it will not allow Iran to ‘hold the global economy hostage’. An instrument announced by one party, unacknowledged by the second and pre-rejected by the third is not a mediated pause. The channel has been at 5/5 since 9 July and can register none of it (§9.7).

UNTESTABLE AS WRITTEN (§9.39) — the test needs a when-issued level Treasury does not publish, so it returns NO state at all and is excluded from Stage 4 in both directions. It is neither armed nor not-armed, and recording it as ‘not armed’ would be the false negative the rule exists to prevent. Treasury’s own tentative schedule has 9 September as a SHORT-END CASH-MANAGEMENT operation, nominal coupons 1Mo–2Y, up to $12.5bn; the 10Y–20Y liquidity-support operation is 10 SEPTEMBER. The release announcing the increase says ‘effective September 9’, which is consistent only if it refers to the ANNOUNCEMENT date of the 10 September operation. Both readings are published and neither is resolved; the updated schedule promised in that release is NOT PUBLISHED — the issuer committed to publish and has not, which is a fact about the world and not about the fetch. Read the allotment composition, not an unsourceable tail (§9.29, §9.40). A2.3.4

ARMED continuously since the 28 August close — SIX consecutive closes, ONE arming — and the run does NOT extend this edition, because 7 SEPTEMBER PRODUCED NO CLOSE. The seventh is decided on the 8 September close, which does not exist at the cut. 30-year 5.2423% clearing by 4.23 bp; 10-year 4.7821% clearing by 13.21 bp. (!) On the 8 September MARK both legs clear by 4.44 and 13.62 bp — which would END three consecutive narrowings on the 30-year leg — but a mark arms nothing and the ordinals are NOT advanced on one. Ordinals UNCHANGED. Across 29 July to 4 September B has armed SIX times and lapsed FIVE — eleven states, ten changes — and the current arming is the sixth, running six closes. (!) §9.49, the recorded DEFECT, stands unchanged for want of a session: B has been satisfied across SIX closes spanning THREE distinct curve shapes — bear flattener, bear steepener and bull steepener — three of the four configurations available. A test meant to detect long-end stress has returned the same answer through all three

NOT ARMED, and UNRESOLVED SINCE 4 SEPTEMBER — MOVE has no print for 7 or 8 September. On its last close of 73.10 it is 56.90 points below C and 41.92 below the 115.02 war high of 26 March. (!) The Treasury downgrade’s volatility leg is SATISFIED on that close and is NOT satisfied a third session; two sessions of silence are not a third close (§9.9). (!) methodology.intraday: §9.56 — NOW FOUR CLOSES OLD, AND THE SCORED GAP HAS HALVED IN THREE SESSIONS. A trigger written on a continuation series stops being well-defined the moment the basis opens, and the failure is silent. The oil channel’s upgrade is ‘Brent above $95 sustained’. That rule was written and applied through long stretches in which CO2 and COA printed the SAME NUMBER — most recently exactly zero for twenty consecutive sessions to 28 August. Earlier rolls opened a basis too; what is new is a roll that opened one STRADDLING the trigger. Brent rolled on 31 August and the basis ran 2.12, 3.08, 3.54, 3.89, 3.96, then 3.84 and 3.88. On the 7 September close the trigger falls BETWEEN the two series for a FOURTH consecutive session: the scored continuation is $1.84 below it and the active contract $2.00 ABOVE it. ‘Sustained’ has a settled operational meaning here — two consecutive confirmed closes, the test that fired US-inflation 4→5 on 31 July and cut oil 2→1 on 3 July. The active contract has now closed above $95 FOUR times in succession, so on that series the upgrade condition is met in full and has been since the 3 September close. (!) THE MATERIAL CHANGE THIS EDITION IS THE SIZE OF WHAT IS LEFT. The scored gap has run $3.37, $2.68, $1.84 across three sessions, and $1.84 is the nearest this series has closed to its trigger since it was last ABOVE it on 24 July. The hold rests on nothing except which of two rising series the rule happens to be written on, and the remaining gap is narrower than the series’ own recent daily range. That is stated plainly rather than dressed up: what settles this is not an argument but two closes. Three things follow and all three remain the practice. (a) The channel is held on the scored continuation, and the alternative reading is published in the EDITION rather than buried here, because a reader checking a screen quote for ‘Brent’ will find the active contract. (b) The rule is NOT moved to whichever series would fire it — the §9.26 discipline. (c) The problem is disclosed as an open methodological question and NOT decided under the pressure of a fired trigger, which is the §9.16 precedent. The general form, which will recur: any threshold expressed as an absolute level on a rolling series has an undefined region as wide as the basis, and the basis is zero exactly when nobody is looking at it. ¶ §9.51 — CARRIED FORWARD, UNCHANGED AND UNSETTLED, and STILL six observations deep because 7 September produced no close. When a defective test is met a second time by a different mechanism, record the MECHANISM, not a verdict. §9.49 recorded Threshold B’s 28 August arming as a defect: a long-end stress test tripped by an 11.14 bp front-end move in which the 30-year contributed 1.25 bp. On 31 August B held on a bear STEEPENER in which the 30-year contributed the largest move on the curve; on 1 September on a bear FLATTENER in which it contributed the smallest; on 2 and 3 September on a BULL STEEPENER twice; and on 4 September on a bear flattener again, in which the 30-year was the ONLY tenor to FALL. (!) The run did NOT extend this edition: there is no 7 September close, so the ordinals are unchanged and the seventh is decided on 8 September. (!) The written test has now returned the same answer through three of the four configurations available, in both directions, and on the latest occasion it was satisfied while its own long-end leg moved TOWARD the threshold, the margin narrowing 4.65 to 4.23 bp — the test held open by the leg it was not written about. That is not ambiguity observed twice but six times, and it strengthens rather than resolves the original complaint. (!) A second observation sharpens it further, and it is new this edition: the two legs DIVERGED for the first time in the run — the 30-year margin narrowed a third consecutive close to 4.23 bp while the 10-year’s WIDENED to 13.21 bp — so a single test is now being held open by the leg it was not written about. The open question is unchanged and is not settled here: whether B should be conditioned on a long-end CONTRIBUTION rather than a long-end LEVEL. ¶ Restatements and comparability. Vendor restatements are normal and make absolute levels non-comparable across editions, though directional analysis is continuous. A contract roll does the same thing to a continuation series silently, which is why the basis check is a standing check. The dual gasoline series is never re-based: AUTMUSAG is the scored reference and preserves the $3.52 anchor and the $4.75 trigger; USRFRUSA is corroboration only; AAA’s published headline is a third series and is never compared with either. The pre-war anchor is the 27 February 2026 close, re-verified field by field every edition; it is unchanged to date. FOUR OPEN ITEMS REMAIN DISCLOSED RATHER THAN DECIDED. (1) FIRST IN LINE AND SHARPER THAN LAST EDITION: §9.56, the oil trigger’s ambiguity across the roll — $2.68 below on the scored series and $1.28 through on the active one, with three consecutive closes through on the active series and, for the first time, both series moving the same way. (2) Threshold B’s long-end LEVEL versus long-end CONTRIBUTION question, per §9.49 and §9.51, now six observations deep with diverging legs and a narrowing 30-year margin. (3) §9.57, the reconciliation of the scored gasoline series to any published construction, open and un-advanceable this edition. (4) The US-inflation channel’s firing-versus-downgrade gap, no longer dormant: the firing trigger has held four closes but the margin has narrowed to 0.82 bp while the downgrade sits 16.62 bp lower. The oil channel’s own separate asymmetry stands unchanged: its downgrade is written as a mediated pause AND ‘a close’ at or below $72.48 while its upgrade requires a SUSTAINED break, which as written makes the downgrade’s PRICE limb easier to trip than the upgrade’s, though the downgrade also requires a mediated pause and is not therefore the easier test overall.
